module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Describe AI as a broad term for systems that do thinking-like tasks
outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
intro: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks we usually connect with human thinking, such as recognizing speech, sorting photos, predicting what comes next, recommending a song, or writing a paragraph. It is an umbrella term, not one machine: a spam filter, a map app's travel-time estimate and a chatbot can all be called AI, yet they work differently and do different jobs. Calling something "AI" does not tell you how well it works or what it can do. To understand a tool, ask what task it performs, what it takes in, and what it gives back.
prompt: Which description fits this course's meaning of AI?
choices: A. Any computer program at all, including a basic pocket calculator | B. A single website that answers questions in a chat window | C. One specific robot that thinks in exactly the same way as a person | D. A broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with human thinking
correct_answer: A broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with human thinking
feedback: AI is an umbrella term for many kinds of systems that do thinking-like tasks.
wrong_choices: A: AI refers to tasks like recognizing, predicting, recommending and generating | B: chatbots are only one kind of AI | C: AI is a broad group, not one robot

module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Look past an "AI" label when a decision matters
outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
intro: Because "AI" is a broad label, it is used loosely. Marketers may call a simple fixed rule "AI" to sound modern, and some tools that do use learned patterns never mention AI at all. Two products both described as "AI-powered" can differ greatly in quality, cost and risk. When a claim matters, for example when a school, employer or bank says AI helps make a decision, look past the label: ask what the system does, what information it uses, how it was tested, and who checks its results. A label is a starting point for questions, not an answer.
prompt: A budgeting app calls itself "AI-powered," but it only applies one fixed rule: save 10 percent of each deposit. What is the best conclusion?
choices: A. It is more reliable because it says "AI-powered" | B. The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work | C. It must be learning from millions of other users' data | D. It cannot work, since it is not "real" AI
correct_answer: The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work
feedback: Labels are used loosely; look at what the system actually does.
wrong_choices: A: a label is not evidence | C: nothing suggests learning | D: a fixed rule can work fine

module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Tell written rules from learned patterns
outcome_title: Tell software that follows rules a person wrote from a system whose behavior comes from patterns learned from examples
intro: Some software follows RULES that a person wrote: "If the total is over 50 dollars, apply free shipping." Every step was decided in advance, so you can read the rule to see why the program acted. Other systems LEARN PATTERNS from examples. A spam filter shown thousands of emails marked "spam" or "not spam" adjusts itself until it sorts new emails well. No one wrote a rule for every case; its behavior comes from the examples it learned from. Rule-based software is predictable but cannot handle cases its rules miss. Learned systems handle messy, varied input but can make surprising mistakes.
prompt: A checkout page gives free shipping whenever an order is over 50 dollars. How was this behavior most likely produced?
choices: A. It learned from many past orders | B. It copied what a chatbot suggested | C. A person wrote a rule for it | D. It guessed the amount at random
correct_answer: A person wrote a rule for it
feedback: A fixed "if over 50, then free" step is a written rule.
wrong_choices: A: a fixed threshold is a written rule | B: nothing suggests a chatbot is involved | D: the result is consistent, not random

module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Explain how AI, machine learning and deep learning nest
outcome_title: Explain machine learning and deep learning as nested ideas, with deep learning using many-layered neural networks
intro: MACHINE LEARNING is a way of building AI in which a system improves at a task by learning patterns from data instead of following only hand-written rules. DEEP LEARNING is one kind of machine learning. It uses NEURAL NETWORKS: many connected layers of simple math units. Each layer passes numbers to the next, and early layers pick up simple features while later layers combine them into more complex ones. "Deep" means many layers, not deep understanding. So the ideas nest like boxes: deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI. Not all AI uses machine learning, and not all machine learning is deep learning.
prompt: How are AI, machine learning and deep learning related?
choices: A. They are three different words for exactly the same thing | B. AI is part of deep learning, which is part of machine learning | C. Deep learning is part of machine learning, which is part of AI | D. Machine learning and deep learning are unrelated to AI
correct_answer: Deep learning is part of machine learning, which is part of AI
feedback: The groups nest: deep learning inside machine learning inside AI.
wrong_choices: A: each is a narrower group | B: the nesting is reversed | D: both are kinds of AI

intro: A MODEL is the trained part of an AI system: the learned patterns that turn input into output. A PRODUCT (an app, website or feature) wraps a model with other parts: a screen to type in, instructions the company adds, safety filters, tools such as web search, saved settings, and usage limits. The same model can sit inside several products that behave differently, and one product can switch models over time. So "this chatbot did X" does not mean every chatbot does X, and a product's feature, like saving files or browsing the web, may come from the product, not from the model itself.

feedback: The model is the learned core; the product wraps it.

intro: A MODEL is the trained part of an AI system: the learned patterns that turn input into output. A PRODUCT (an app, website or feature) wraps a model with other parts: a screen to type in, instructions the company adds, safety filters, tools such as web search, saved settings, and usage limits. The same model can sit inside several products that behave differently, and one product can switch models over time. So "this chatbot did X" does not mean every chatbot does X, and a product's feature, like saving files or browsing the web, may come from the product, not from the model itself.
prompt: Two apps use the same model but behave differently. What is the most likely reason?
choices: A. Each product adds its own instructions, tools and limits | B. The model must be broken in one of the apps | C. Products cannot share a model, so this cannot happen | D. Models change randomly each time you open an app
correct_answer: Each product adds its own instructions, tools and limits
feedback: Products wrap the same model in different ways.
wrong_choices: B: differences usually come from the products | C: they can share models | D: not the usual reason

section_skill: Use human comparisons carefully
outcome_title: Use human comparisons carefully: say where a comparison helps, where it misleads, and why abilities can be uneven
intro: People often compare AI with humans: "it reads," "it thinks," "it is like a student." Comparisons can help explain a new idea, but they can also mislead. A system may beat experts at one narrow task, such as spotting a pattern in thousands of images, yet fail at something a child finds easy, like counting objects in an unusual picture. Its abilities can be UNEVEN in ways a human's are not, so success on one task does not predict success on a nearby task. Treat a human comparison as a starting point, then check how the system actually performs on the task you care about.
prompt: A system scores better than doctors at spotting one type of spot on X-rays. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: A. It will also be excellent at reading patient notes | B. It can now replace doctors for all medical decisions | C. It must understand medicine as well as a doctor | D. It did well on that narrow task; other tasks need checks
correct_answer: It did well on that narrow task; other tasks need checks
feedback: Narrow success does not transfer automatically.
wrong_choices: A: nearby tasks can differ | B: one task does not predict others | C: performance is not understanding

outcome_title: Use human comparisons carefully: say where a comparison helps, where it misleads, and why abilities can be uneven
intro: A pocket calculator multiplies huge numbers instantly, faster than any person, yet it cannot tell a cat from a dog. A toddler easily tells a cat from a dog but cannot multiply 27 by 43. section_skill: Describe what was observed instead of "smart" or "dumb"
outcome_title: Use human comparisons carefully: say where a comparison helps, where it misleads, and why abilities can be uneven
intro: Human comparisons shape trust. If a system "sounds like a person," people may assume it has human judgment, feelings or common sense. Some language models are trained to sound helpful and friendly, which can make errors easier to miss. On the other hand, dismissing a system as "just a machine" can hide real abilities and real risks. A better habit is to describe what was observed: "It summarized these ten reports accurately but invented one date," rather than "It is smart" or "It is dumb." Specific observations can be checked.

section_skill: Tell training from inference (using the model)
outcome_title: Tell training (learning patterns from data) from inference (using the finished model on new input)
intro: An AI model has two very different stages. TRAINING is when the model learns: it is shown large amounts of example data and its internal settings are adjusted again and again until its outputs match the examples well. Training happens before you use the model and usually takes a lot of computing power. INFERENCE (or simply "using the model") is when the finished model takes NEW input, such as your question or photo, and produces an output. During ordinary use the model's learned settings do not change. Typing a question into an app is inference, not training.
prompt: A company shows a model millions of labeled photos and adjusts it until it sorts them well. Which stage is this?
choices: A. Inference, because the model is being used on photos | B. Inference, because the photos are labeled | C. Neither, because sorting photos is not AI | D. Training
correct_answer: Training
feedback: Adjusting the model to match examples is training.
wrong_choices: A: it is still learning from examples | B: labels are used for learning | C: sorting photos is a common AI task

The TEST SET is kept aside and used only at the end to measure how well the finished model does on examples it has never seen. If test examples leak into training, the test score looks better than the model really is, because the model may have learned those exact answers. A trustworthy result comes from examples that stayed unseen.

OVERFITTING is the opposite: the model fits its training examples so closely, including their accidents and noise, that it does worse on new ones. intro: A LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL (LLM) is a model trained on enormous amounts of text to do one core job: given some text, predict a likely next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, produces sentences, answers, stories or code. Because it learned from so much writing, an LLM can imitate many styles and often produces useful, relevant text. But predicting likely text is not the same as looking up facts or reasoning like a person. An LLM has no built-in way to check truth, so its output can be plausible and wrong. "Large" refers to the size of the model and its training data.

section_skill: Explain probabilities and why answers vary
outcome_title: Explain that a language model chooses among likely next tokens, so the same request can produce different answers
intro: At each step, a language model gives every possible next token a PROBABILITY: how likely it is to come next. After "The sky is," the token "blue" might get a high probability and "green" a low one. The model then picks a token, often by SAMPLING, which means choosing at random but weighted by those probabilities. That is why the same request can produce different answers on different tries. Some products let users or developers adjust settings, sometimes called temperature, that make choices more predictable or more varied. Variation is useful for brainstorming but means you should not expect identical answers every time.

outcome_title: Explain that a language model chooses among likely next tokens, so the same request can produce different answers
intro: Variation has practical effects. If you ask the same factual question twice and get two different numbers, at most one can be right, and maybe neither, so the difference is a signal to check a source, not to pick the one you like. When you need consistency, such as the same format for 100 product descriptions, give clear instructions and a template, and check the results, because even predictable settings do not guarantee identical outputs in every product. When you want ideas, variation is a feature: ask for several options at once.

feedback: Different answers to a factual question signal the need to check.
wrong_choices: A: agreement is not proof | B: averaging guesses is not a check | C: preference is not evidence

intro: A model can only consider a limited amount of text at once, called its CONTEXT WINDOW, measured in tokens. The context usually includes instructions the product adds, the conversation so far, any files or pasted text, and the reply being written. When a long conversation or document exceeds the window, something has to give: depending on the product, older messages may be dropped or shortened, part of a file may be left out, or the request may be refused. section_skill: Tell built-in knowledge from supplied or retrieved information
outcome_title: Tell knowledge learned in training (with a cutoff date) from information supplied or retrieved during a request
intro: A model's built-in knowledge comes from its training data, which stops at a TRAINING CUTOFF date. It does not know about events after that date unless the information is SUPPLIED or RETRIEVED during your request: you paste a document, or the product runs a web search and adds the results to the context. These are different: built-in knowledge is patterns frozen at training time and may be incomplete or wrong, while supplied or retrieved text is current material the model reads now, which is only as good as its source. When an answer depends on recent facts, know which kind you are getting.

section_skill: Explain why a product's behavior is more than its model
outcome_title: Explain that a product adds its own instructions, settings, tools and limits, so a general description of LLMs cannot predict one product's behavior
intro: A general description of language models cannot tell you exactly how a particular product will behave. Products add their own layers: SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS the company writes (for example, "be brief" or "do not give medical diagnoses"), SAFETY FILTERS, TOOLS such as web search, code running or file reading, SETTINGS, and LIMITS on length or usage. Two products built on similar models can therefore refuse different requests, format answers differently, or have different abilities. To know what a product does, test it on your task and read its documentation.

intro: A general description of language models cannot tell you exactly how a particular product will behave. Products add their own layers: SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS the company writes (for example, "be brief" or "do not give medical diagnoses"), SAFETY FILTERS, TOOLS such as web search, code running or file reading, SETTINGS, and LIMITS on length or usage. Two products built on similar models can therefore refuse different requests, format answers differently, or have different abilities. To know what a product does, test it on your task and read its documentation.
prompt: A product can read your spreadsheet files. Where does that ability come from?
choices: A. The model memorized your spreadsheet in training | B. Every language model reads files by itself | C. Your spreadsheet program sends answers automatically | D. A file-reading tool the product provides
correct_answer: A file-reading tool the product provides
feedback: Tools are added by the product.
wrong_choices: A: not possible | B: tools are product features | C: not how it works

feedback: The model is the shared ingredient.
